Context: During the early 1890s, the American Railway Union, led by Eugene V. Debs, launched a boycott of all Pullman cars on all railroads in response to corporate actions. ARU members across the nation refused to switch Pullman cars onto trains, leading to disciplinary actions and a strike starting on June 26, 1894. Within four days, 125,000 workers on twenty-nine railroads had quit work. Strikers and their supporters also engaged in riots and sabotage. The railroads secured the appointment of Edwin Walker, general counsel for the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railway, as a special federal attorney to address the strike. Walker obtained a federal court injunction based on the Sherman Anti-Trust Act against the union leaders' support of the boycott. Despite this, ARU leaders ignored the injunction, and federal troops were deployed. United States Marshals and some 2,000 United States Army troops, led by Nelson Miles and ordered by President Grover Cleveland, ended the strike since it interfered with the delivery of U.S. Mail. The strike resulted in 13 deaths and 57 injuries, and approximately $340,000 in property damage. Debs was imprisoned for six months for defying the federal court order, leading to the dissolution of the ARU.
